uses: Elderflower tea, drunk hot at bedtime, is a traditional way to meet the first signs of a cold and to encourage a good sweat. Elderflower water was an old-fashioned skin and eye wash, said to fade freckles and soothe sunburn. The blossoms were also worked into ointments for chapped hands and chilblains. In the kitchen they flavor cordials and wines.
taste: Lightly floral and slightly bitter when fresh
caution_pregnancy: Safety during pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established. Not enough is known; avoid. The EMA does not recommend elderflower medicines then.
caution_medications: The EMA reports no known interactions. Some herbs and medicines do interact, so check with a pharmacist before combining elderflower with any medicine.
caution_conditions: Avoid it if you are allergic to elderflower. Medicinal use isn't established for children under 12. With a cold, see a doctor if you become short of breath, run a fever or cough up discolored phlegm. Use only the flowers: elder leaves, stems and roots are poisonous, so strip the blossoms from their stalks.
caution_duration: If cold symptoms last longer than a week, see a doctor or qualified practitioner. None of our sources describes long-term use.
caution_topical: The EMA monograph covers use by mouth only and gives no skin warning. Not enough is known about skin use; stop if irritation appears.
garden_harvest_timing: Cut the flat cream flower heads in early summer when they have just fully opened, on a dry day; the bloom lasts only about three weeks.
garden_water: Moist, rich soil with good drainage
notes: Comes from the same shrub as elderberry; every head you cut is fruit you won't get later, so leave some to ripen. Flowers draw butterflies. See the elderberry entry for the folklore of the elder tree.
